Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00249

Once we see that existence is not a general kind because it has no feature that divides it into species, the same reasoning shows that it is not a species either. Nor is its reality a universal nature that could be divided by other distinguishing conditions, such as features added from outside to make an individual distinct. Features added from outside, such as individual circumstances, may cause a thing to become actual, but they do not make up its essence. A species needs a distinguishing feature not in order to be described by its general kind, but in order to become an actual species. In the same way, an individual does not need an individualizing feature in order to be described by its species; it needs one in order to exist as an individual. But this can only happen with things whose reality is not existence itself. If existence needed something added to it in order to become distinct, that added feature would have to be part of the essence of the species. So existence itself is not a general kind or a species.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00250

Nor is existence a universal concept in any of the other ways that universal ideas are classified. Even the other three kinds of universal idea ultimately reduce to a general kind or a species. This shows that existences are real, individual things, distinct in themselves. They are not general kinds, species, or universal concepts; nor are they individual things made distinct by something added to them. They are distinct through themselves, not through a separate feature or an incidental quality.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00251

Since existence has no general kind and no distinguishing feature, it has no strict definition. And since it has no definition, it cannot be proved by demonstration, because definitions and proofs share corresponding parts, as we have already indicated. We know existence either through direct awareness of it or by reasoning from its effects and necessary features. The second kind of knowledge is only partial and indirect.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00252
Existence itself has no cause in any sense
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00253

You can now see why existence, considered in itself, cannot be made of parts. That is true whether the supposed parts exist outside the mind, are found in thought, or arise only when we analyze a thing. Look at what makes up the essence of a thing. Do you not find that its reality depends on those parts—not because it is an effect they produce, but because its very nature depends on them? The essence of the whole is simply the essence of its components, whether we consider them in the outside world, in the mind, or in reality as such.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00254

If existence itself were made from basic elements joined together, each element—or at least one of them—would either be existence itself or something other than existence. In the first case, existence would already have come from a source before itself. In the second, the assumed reality of existence would be something beyond that nonexistence element, so the supposed whole would reduce to one of its parts or to something outside them.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00255

There is another problem: something other than existence would have to come before existence by means of existence, which is plainly impossible. The reality of existence would also have to be present in its components before it was present in the thing made from them. A thing would then exist before itself, and existence would depend on itself. So existence itself cannot be made of distinct parts, like matter and form, or divided into things with the same reality and existence. In short, its reality cannot be analyzed as one thing and another. Pure reality cannot be repeated or doubled, either outside the mind, in the mind, or in any other sense.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00256

Once you see that nothing other than existence can come before existence through existence, it becomes clear that existence as such is established by itself and exists through itself. It is its own reality and its own existence. In itself, it depends on nothing; dependence belongs only to its particular expressions and later forms. Existence as existence has no agent from which it comes, no matter that turns into it, no subject in which it exists, no form it takes on, and no goal it serves. Rather, it is the source of all causes, the form of all forms, and the goal of all goals—the final goal and pure good toward which all realities and essences tend. Existence is therefore above every kind of cause: it has no cause by which it exists, no cause from which it comes, no cause through which it arises, no subject in which it exists, and no goal for which it exists. We will explain each of these points later.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00257
Objections and answers
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00258

Several objections remain to the claim that existence has real instances outside the mind. One comes from Suhrawardi's The Book of Hints: If existence is a feature of essence in the outside world, then essence must receive it. Does essence exist after, before, or at the same time as existence? If it exists afterward, then existence was already independent of essence, so essence cannot be receiving it as a feature. If essence exists beforehand, then it exists before existence. If the two exist together, essence exists alongside existence, not through it, and must have another existence of its own. All these consequences are false, so the original claim must be false.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00259

The answer is to choose the last option: essence and existence are together in the outside world. The very existence through which essence exists also makes it present at the same time; no second existence is needed. This is like the simultaneity of a movement and the time in which it occurs. That time itself makes them simultaneous; we do not need a second time, which would lead to an endless chain.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00260

When the mind calls an essence existent, it is making a judgment. The essence is not receiving existence as it might receive some other feature—as though the essence had one existence and the feature another. Outside the mind, essence and existence are one. Neither comes before the other, and they are not even “together” in the ordinary sense just discussed. It is only the mind that treats existence as a feature of essence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00261

A careful scholar has explained this as follows: When an existence proceeds from the First Source, it has an identity distinct from the First. Its being an effect of the First is one idea; its being this particular identity is another. So there are two things the mind can understand. The first is what proceeds from the First, called existence. The second is the identity that necessarily follows from that existence, called essence. In reality, essence follows existence: if the First brought nothing about, there would be no essences. In thought, however, existence follows essence, because we describe the essence as existing. This is what the scholar says.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00262

What he says, together with what we have explained, shows that essence is united with existence in reality, in a certain way. When the mind analyzes them as two ideas, it judges that one is prior in reality and the other is prior in thought. Existence comes first in reality, because it is the original effect of the First Source, while essence is united with and predicated of it—not as a feature that arrives later. Essence comes first in thought because it is the starting point for our judgments about things.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00263

This priority may be through existence or in another sense. As we will see, there is a sixth kind of priority beyond the five familiar kinds: priority in the very nature of a thing. For example, the nature of a general kind comes before the nature of its species, without regard to whether either exists.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00264

The difference between essence and existence, and the claim that essence is described as existing, belong to thought. They do not occur outside the mind. Even in the mind, however, essence is never separate from existence, because being an object of thought is itself a kind of mental existence, just as being in the world is external existence. Still, the mind can consider an essence by itself, without attending to either kind of existence, and then describe it as existing.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00265

You may object: “But thinking of essence in this way is itself a kind of existence. How, then, can essence be said to have that existence, or the general concept of existence that covers it? Must not a thing already exist before it can be described?” The answer is that this act of attention has two sides. On one side, the mind considers essence as stripped of every kind of existence. On the other, it notices that this very act of stripping is itself a kind of existence. From the first point of view, essence is not described as existing; from the second, it is. This causes no contradiction or endless chain.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00266

We can also avoid this complication, since we have established that existence is the very reality of essence, not something that exists in essence as a separate feature. Calling the relation between essence and existence “description” or “attribution” is a broad use of the word. It is not like the relation between a subject and its ordinary qualities. Essence is described as existing more like a simple thing being described through what belongs to it by its nature, not as something separate that later becomes one with existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00267

Here is another objection. If existence were real outside the mind, it would have to belong to an essence. But what sort of essence? If the essence already exists, it must exist before it exists. If it does not exist, existence and nonexistence would belong to it at once. If it is considered apart from both existence and nonexistence, neither could be affirmed of it. Every option is impossible.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00268

The answer is to choose the first option if “existing” and “not existing” mean what is true in reality: existence inheres in an essence that exists, but through that very existence, not through an earlier one. Whiteness, for example, belongs to a white body through that very whiteness, not through some earlier whiteness. If instead “existing” and “not existing” mean what is included in the definition of essence considered in itself, then existence belongs to essence considered without either existence or nonexistence in its definition. This does not mean that reality lacks both opposites, because reality is broader than that limited way of considering essence. Outside the mind, essence must have one or the other. Likewise, whiteness belongs to a body without whiteness or its absence being part of what the body is in itself; in reality, the body must either be white or not white.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00269

The difference between this case and the case of a body receiving whiteness is that a body has an existence before it becomes white, and can therefore be described as white or not white. But outside the mind, essence is identical with existence. It cannot be described as existing in that setting, because description requires at least some difference between the two, even if it does not require one to come before the other. The same mixing of essence and existence happens in the mind, except when the mind deliberately considers both how essence is mixed with existence and how it can be considered apart from it, as explained earlier. We have already seen that no extra relation between them is needed: in reality, essence and existence are one. Essence is united with external existence outside the mind and with mental existence in thought. When the mind considers essence without attending to any kind of existence, it judges them different in thought: the ideas differ, as the ideas of general kind and distinguishing feature differ in simple things, even though they are one in what is made real and in existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00270

A careful scholar makes a similar point: Neither the abstract noun “existence” nor the idea “existent” can be a feature of essence in reality, because for one thing to belong to another, the thing it belongs to must already exist. Essence would then have to exist before it existed.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00271

The idea of “existent” is united with the essences of things, and what is united cannot be an added feature of the other. Nor does existence, as an abstract noun, become a feature of essence even in the mind's analysis. The mind may first consider an essence by itself, without adding anything to it. Even when it later finds the essence to be existent, it does not thereby treat the abstract noun “existence” as a separate feature belonging to it. A descriptive word can apply without the feature from which it is formed existing separately in its subject.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00272

Existence in the sense of “existent” can be attributed to essence in the mind, because the mind considers essence first by itself and then as existent. That is why it says the feature belongs to essence. But existence cannot be an added feature of essence in reality, because the two are one there. Whiteness and existence, for example, are one in reality; there is no relation of one being an added feature of the other. In thought they are two ideas, because the mind can analyze the same thing into an essence it considers first and an existence it considers afterward.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00273

This is the gist of that scholar's argument. An attentive reader will see where it agrees with and differs from what we have established. For him, existence is either the abstract idea expressed by the word “existence” or the general concept “existent”; both are ideas in the mind. For us, existence is a real thing in itself. Still, we agree on one point: the mind treats existence and essence as one in reality and as two in its own analysis.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00274

There are several points in this scholar's argument that can be questioned. A contemporary of the eminent al-Dawani raised some of them, and that critic also has several problems of his own. Pursuing all of them would take us beyond the scope of this book.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00275

Suhrawardi argues in The Philosophy of Illumination and The Book of Hints that nothing exists whose essence is existence itself. We can understand the idea of such a thing and still wonder whether it actually exists. It must therefore have an existence added to its essence. But the same question then applies to that existence, and the chain continues without end. The only way out, he says, is to treat “existence,” when applied to things, as an idea in the mind.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00276

We have already given the answer. The inner reality of existence cannot become an idea inside the mind. The mind grasps an abstract concept of it, but that is only one aspect. To know existence in its full reality is to encounter it directly. Once we do so and grasp its nature, the doubt on which the objection depends falls away.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00277

It is better to use this argument against Aristotelian philosophers, as Suhrawardi does in The Philosophy of Illumination. They argue that existence differs from essence because we can understand an essence and still wonder whether it exists; what we wonder about is not the same as what we understand, nor part of it. So, they say, existence and essence must also differ in reality.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00278

Suhrawardi applies the same argument to existence itself. We can understand the idea “existence”—for example, the existence of a phoenix—without knowing whether it exists in the outside world. Existence would then need a further existence, which would need another in turn—an endless series of existences assumed to be present together. But the answer we gave to Suhrawardi applies just as well to this original argument: the doubt concerns an idea in the mind, not reality itself. This pulls the ground from under both arguments.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00279

Suhrawardi also argues that if existence were an added feature of essence in the outside world, there would have to be a relation between them. That relation would itself need an existence, and its existence would need a relation of its own, continuing without end.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00280

The answer is that these relations exist only in the mind, not in reality outside it. The chain therefore ends when the mind stops considering them. As we have already explained, essence and existence are not different in reality at all. The mind can analyze some existing things into essence and existence, then consider one as describing the other, as we discussed earlier.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00281

Suhrawardi raises another objection. If existence is real but is not a substance, it must be a feature of something. If so, it belongs to a substance and counts as a quality, according to the philosophers in Aristotle’s school. A quality is a stable feature that we can understand without dividing it into parts or relating it to something outside it. But they also say that a subject must exist before an accident can belong to it. The subject would then have to exist before existence—a contradiction, since this would mean that existence comes before existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00282

Existence would not, then, be the broadest of all things. Quality and accident would each be broader than it in one respect. And if existence were an accident, it would depend on a subject. To say that it depends on a subject means that it exists in that subject and needs it in order to be real. But the subject itself exists through existence. So each would depend on the other, which is impossible.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00283

Here is the answer. Philosophers define each basic kind of thing by its nature and by how it exists outside the mind. A substance, for example, exists without being in a subject. A quantity can, by its own nature, be equal or unequal to another quantity. Quality and the other basic kinds are defined in the same way. So existence itself is not a substance, quality, or anything else of that sort: it is not universal. As we have said, particular existences are actual realities, each distinct in itself. They do not fall under a universal essence such as a general kind, a species, or a definition.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00284

Existence is not an accident in the sense of something that inheres in the essence it makes real. It is accidental in another sense, and united with essence in a certain way. Even if we call it an accident, that does not make it a quality, because it is neither universal nor general. What is universal and applies broadly to existing things is the abstract idea of existence in the mind, from which the idea “existent” is formed. This abstract concept also differs from other accidents: an accident exists in itself in the same way that it exists in its subject, but the existence of existence is the very existence of essence, not some further existence added to it. So existence does not need a subject in order to be real, and the circle of dependence disappears. In our view, the existence of a substance is substantial through that substance's own substantiality, not through another substance; and the existence of an accident is accidental through that accident's own nature, not through another accident. As we have seen, existence does not describe essence as a separate feature in reality. The mind sees that relation only when it analyzes things.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00285
Clarification: Existence and light
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00286

From what we have explained, we can see that the word “light” has two uses. Sometimes it means the act or state of lighting something up. In that sense, it has no existence outside the mind; it is an abstract idea. At other times, it means what is clear in itself and makes other things clear: God, the intellects, the souls, and the kinds of light we can understand or see, such as starlight and the light of lamps. In this sense, light exists in reality, not merely in the mind. The same word is used for these different realities in related senses. In its first use, “light” is a general idea that applies to many examples. In its second, it is the very reality of light, with different degrees of completeness and incompleteness, strength and weakness. In that sense, it is not a general idea or an individual thing that needs some further mark to make it distinct. Light is pure actuality, distinction, clarity, and manifestation.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00287

Why, then, does light sometimes fail to appear or shine brightly? Either our power of perception, whether sight or understanding, is too weak, or the light is mixed with darkness as it unfolds through levels of limitation and material weakness. For every level at which light is weaker and less complete than the fullest perfection of light—which has no limit in majesty, beauty, or splendor—there is a corresponding level of darkness and nonexistence, called a possible essence. You will learn more about this later.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00288

Existence, too, is used in two ways. It can mean the abstract idea the mind draws from things, one of the concepts that has no reality in itself outside the mind. This is existence as a predicate. Or it can mean the real fact that, through itself, keeps nonexistence away from its own reality and, by joining with an essence, keeps nonexistence away from that essence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00289

There is no doubt that adding the abstract idea of existence—which has no reality in itself—to an essence does not keep that essence from being nonexistent. It does so only because the abstract idea points to what it depends on: real existence. That real existence may be the self-sufficient existence that must be, or the contingent existence that depends on another. The very identity of contingent existences consists in their dependence and connection with the existence that must be. Their meanings are not separate realities to which a connection with God is added later, as happens with possible essences, each of which has its own nature and is then connected to God through real existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00290

Those real existences are nothing but aspects of His essence, manifestations of His highest attributes, flashes of His light and beauty, and rays of His splendor. We will prove this later, God willing. For now, our concern is to show that existence in every thing is real, apart from the abstract idea of “being”—whether we mean being attributed to existence itself or being attributed to an essence. The abstract idea of being relates to real existence as “humanity” relates to “a human being,” and “whiteness” to “white.” Its relation to an essence is more like “humanity” to “someone who laughs,” or “whiteness” to “snow.”
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00291

What produces an effect, and what is produced, are real existences: actual realities that exist in themselves. They are not abstract ideas, which everyone agrees exist only in the mind and not outside it. Nor are they bare, general essences that have never, in their own nature, known what it is to exist. As we will explain in the discussion of creation, what is made—the effect that follows directly from the maker—is a mode of existence brought about by direct creation, not an essence. And the maker, insofar as it is a maker, is a level of existence, not one essence among others.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00292

The point is that what exists outside the mind is not just essences without actual existence, as many later thinkers have supposed. The reality they say comes before every description and prevents nonexistence cannot be a mental abstraction with no reality of its own. A mental abstraction cannot keep something from being nonexistent or come before its being described. From that power to prevent nonexistence, and that priority to every description, we know that existence has a reality in itself. This reality is existence and actuality itself; it is not some other thing that happens to exist, as we have said. How far these thinkers have strayed, when they claim that existence means nothing more than an abstract idea in the mind and deny that it has a reality outside the mind!
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00293

What we have said also answers the claim of a careful scholar that existence cannot truly come before essences become real, because existence means nothing real and is only an idea the mind draws from things. Our reply is that what comes before essences are made real and established is existence in its true, external sense—not the abstract idea in the mind. One proof that existence is real outside the mind comes from what Avicenna says in the Metaphysics of The Healing:
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00294

If something always exists through another, then it is not simple in its reality. What it has through itself is not what it has through another, and its identity is made up of both together in existence. For this reason, nothing but the Necessary One is free, in itself, from what is potential and possible. He is one; everything else is a compound.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00295

Avicenna's point is that what a maker brings about is neither the essence nor the abstract idea of existence, but something real beyond them. He does not mean that essence and existence each have a separate existence. Existence itself is real, while essence is united with it in a certain way. No one disputes that existence and essence differ in thought, not in external reality.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00296

Once this point is established, we can say that what makes any two things one is existence. This holds whether they are one in their reality, as a human being and existence are; one in the way a human being and animal are; or one by an added feature, as a human being and something white are. What makes a human being and existence one is the existence that belongs to the human being in its own right. What makes a human being and animal one is the existence that belongs to both in their own right. What makes a human being and something white one is the existence that belongs to the human being in its own right and to whiteness only indirectly.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00297

So two things that are united cannot both be separate, fully real beings; otherwise they would not be one. Rather, the same existence is related to both in some way. At least one of them—and sometimes both—must therefore be an idea drawn from reality, while what makes them one is real.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00298

The unity of essence and existence must be understood in one of two ways. Either existence is only an abstract idea and essences are the real things, as those who cannot see the path of direct insight believe; or essences are abstract ideas and existence is the real thing outside the mind. The second is the sound view.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00299

In short, real existence is one in reality and kind, simple, with no general kind or distinguishing feature, and not universal or particular. Its different forms and distinctions come from within itself, not from something added to it. Yet existence is shared by all essences, united with them, and truly applies to them because of that union. In real existence, what “existence” means is the same as what “existent” means: as the source of the idea “existent,” it is itself what exists; as what gives rise to the idea of existence and makes essences real, it is existence. Both real existence and the abstract idea of existence are shared among essences, but only the abstract idea is universal and general. It is a mental concept that applies broadly, like thinghood, knowability, or possibility in general.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00300

Real existence is different. It is reality and distinctness itself, so it needs nothing else to make it definite. When united with an essence, it makes that essence definite too, bringing it out of vagueness and concealment. Real existence is clear through itself in every way, and it makes everything else clear. Through it, with it, in it, and from it, essences become visible. If existence did not shine within the things that are, and reveal itself through them, they would have no appearance or existence at all. They would remain hidden behind the veil of nonexistence and darkness. We know that, in themselves and within their own limits, they are bare of existence and manifestation; these come to them from elsewhere. In themselves, they are always empty of reality, at every time and every level—as the Persian verse says: “The possible being's dark face has never left it, in either world.”
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00301

This explains the Persian verse about possibility's dark face in both worlds. When existence reveals itself at each level of the universe and appears in each of its different forms, a corresponding level of possible things and fixed realities appears as well. The farther these levels descend from the source of existence, the more nonexistence and darkness take on the appearance of existence and light. Existence is more veiled by the things in which it appears, more hidden in the forms through which it is revealed, and more tinted by the colors of the world.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00302

Every stage of manifestation brings a descent from a higher level of perfection, greatness, and light. The more a level is veiled and hidden, the more clearly it appears to weak powers of perception. With stronger perception, the opposite is true. Think of the different levels of sunlight: what a bat can see is not what a human eye can see. That is why ordinary people find it easier to perceive bodies, whose existence is faint, than immaterial lights, whose existence and brightness are far stronger. Nothing has greater existence and light than the One who brings it all about: the Light of lights, the existence of all existences.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00303

Yet God's existence and self-disclosure have no limit in strength, duration, or extent. Precisely for that reason, our eyes cannot see Him and our minds cannot contain Him. The senses and imagination turn away; the intellect and understanding fall short. Weak powers of perception grasp lower forms of existence, which are accompanied by nonexistence and hidden qualities, and veiled by the many colors and opposing features of possible essences. In their reality, these forms have one meaning. They differ only in how strong or weak, complete or incomplete, high or low they are, according to the levels through which the one simple reality appears. We will make this clearer when we discuss how existence varies by degree.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00304

If our powers of perception were not weak and limited, we would expect the most complete existence and the brightest manifestation to be most present and clear to us. Since the Necessary One possesses existence and light in the highest degree, He should be the most evident of all things to us. But we find the opposite. This shows that the difficulty lies not in God—for He is supreme in greatness, encompassing all things, and radiant beyond measure—but in our minds. They are weak, immersed in matter, and entangled with nonexistence and darkness, so they struggle to know Him as He truly is. The sheer fullness of His perfection overwhelms them.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00305

He is distant from us only because, by our own nature, we are far from the source of existence and the spring of light and manifestation. In reality, His greatness, vast mercy, penetrating light, and infinity make Him nearer to us than anything else, as God says: “We are nearer to him than his jugular vein,” and: “When My servants ask you about Me, I am near.” So His hiddenness comes from the very intensity of His manifestation: He is hidden because He is so fully apparent.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00306

The clearer our perception becomes, and the farther we move from bodily attachments and material veils, the more strongly the lights of the First Reality and the manifestations of His beauty and majesty appear to us. Even then, we cannot know Him completely or grasp Him as He is, because our powers of perception are finite while His existence and light are without limit. All faces bow before the Living, the One who sustains all.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00307

We should also understand this: existences do not differ in their own reality except in completeness and incompleteness, priority and what follows, clarity and concealment. Yet each level brings with it certain possible features and qualities. Philosophers call these “essences”; mystics and those who know through direct insight call them “fixed realities.” Consider sunlight shining through pieces of colored glass. The colors come from the glass; the light has no color in itself and differs only in how brightly it shines. Anyone who stops at the glass and its colors, and lets them hide the real light and its different degrees of manifestation, will fail to see the light. That is what happens when people treat essences as independently real and existence as nothing but an idea in the mind.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00308

When someone sees the colors of light and understands that they come from the glass, while light itself has no color, the light becomes visible to them. They see that its different degrees appear in the forms of things according to what each form can receive. The same is true of someone who understands that the levels of existence are flashes of the true, Necessary Light. They appear in the forms of fixed realities, take on the colors of possible essences, and are veiled by created forms, so that the necessary divine reality is hidden from view.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00309

You should know that our recognition of many levels of existence, and our use of that language while we discuss and teach them, does not conflict with what we will establish later, God willing: that existence and what exists are one in their essence and reality. This is the view of the saints and the great mystics, whose knowledge comes through direct insight and certainty. We will give a decisive proof that the many existences, despite their differences, are levels of the First Reality's self-definition, manifestations of His light, and aspects of His own reality. They are not independent things or separate realities. Keep this account in mind until its proof is given.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00310

Some groups hold that real existence is a single individual: God's own essence. Essences, they say, are real, and for them to exist is simply for them to be related to God's necessary existence. On this view, existence is one particular reality, while “existent” is a general idea with many instances: all the things that exist. This view is attributed to the spiritual insight of the divine philosophers. I see several problems with it. First, it cannot be right to say that God's essence itself is the existence of every essence, whether substance or accident. Some individual things have the same essence, yet one exists before another. They cannot be prior to one another if the very same single existence truly belongs to them all.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00311

You might reply: “It is not real existence that comes earlier or later. Rather, one essence is related to it before another.” But a relation, considered simply as a relation, is an idea in the mind. It has no reality or differences of its own; these depend on one of the things related. But if what the relation is directed toward is one, indivisible reality, and the essence related to it has nothing in its own nature that implies priority, posteriority, cause, or effect, then the difference between these relations cannot explain how one thing exists before another.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00312

Nor can one individual of an essence be prior to another, since, in this view, individuals do not become real and actual through existence in themselves or through their own essences. So how could one individual of a single essence be related to the Necessary One earlier than another?
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00313

The second problem is this. If the relation between essences and God is a relation of identity, then God would have many essences besides existence—many different essences, in fact. We will show later that He has no essence other than His very existence. But if the relation is one of dependence, then dependence on something presupposes that both things already exist. Each essence would therefore need its own existence before it could be related to God. There is no doubt that essences are not simply identical with their dependence on something else: we can often think of an essence and still wonder whether it is connected to the First Reality. We can say, however, that the reality of existences is not separate from their dependence and connection, because we cannot settle for an account of existence without knowing the reality of its cause and maker. This follows from rigorous proof, and we will show it in this book, God willing.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00314

The third problem is that this view also gives us many existences, just as it gives us many existent things. It says that the existent things are real, while some existences are real—God's existence—and others are abstract ideas—the existences of contingent things. In this, it is no different from the common view held by most later philosophers: the existence of contingent things is an idea in the mind, while God's existence is real because He Himself is what the word “existent” truly refers to. For contingent things, by contrast, existing is only an idea the mind draws from them.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00315

The only difference is that this view calls the abstract idea of existence “relation,” “dependence,” or some other name. So there seems to be no reason to say that, on this view, real existence is one individual while “existent” is a general concept with many examples. In both views, the existence—or the fact of being existent—attributed to things is a mental concept shared by all that exist, whether the source of their existence is their own essence, a relation of dependence, or something else. If “existence” is used in another sense, to mean the reality that exists through itself, then the same word is being used for two different meanings. We will explain the different views about how things exist later.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00316
Chapter — Existence and being a thing
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00317

Some people say that existence is a feature that comes to be attached to an essence that is already a thing, whether it exists or not. This view is extremely weak. The nature of essence is different from the nature of existence, but until an essence exists, we cannot point to it as this particular essence. We can speak of what does not exist only in words. An essence cannot be anything at all—not even itself—until it exists. For to be itself already depends on its being real and existing.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00318

In reality, existence comes first. The mind, however, considers essence first and existence afterward. As we have seen, it is in the mind that essence is described as existing. And a subject, insofar as it is the subject of a description, comes before the description that belongs to it. Hold on to this point; it is valuable.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00319

They also say that features neither exist nor fail to exist; they are neither known nor unknown. Only the essence is known through a feature, while the feature itself is not known. Yet they accept that what is impossible is ruled out, and that there is no third option between denying something and affirming it.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00320

Some people try to place an intermediate status between what exists and what does not. They say that something can be “fixed” in a certain way while still not existing: a possible thing that does not exist outside the mind, existence itself, or a special status they call a “state,” which is neither existent nor nonexistent. Perhaps these people have simply agreed to use a word in a special way. Or perhaps they have overlooked the difference between what exists in the mind and what exists outside it. If by “nonexistent” they mean nonexistent outside the mind, then something may be established in thought while not existing outside it. If they mean anything else, their claim is false, and nothing can be said about it or through it.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00321

One way to expose the problem is to ask: if a possible thing does not exist outside the mind, is its existence affirmed or denied? By their own admission, there is no third option between affirmation and denial. If they deny its existence, then, by their own view, anything denied must be impossible. A possible thing would therefore be impossible, which is absurd. But if they affirm existence of it, and every feature that is affirmed of a thing can be said of it, then the nonexistent thing can be described as existent while it is nonexistent. It would be both existent and nonexistent, which is impossible.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00322

If they refuse to let us describe something by a feature that is affirmed of it, then we must also refuse to call a nonexistent essence a “thing,” even though its thinghood is affirmed of it. Anyone who accepts this result cannot call it a thing, while also claiming that it is a thing. The same problem applies to possibility.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00323

They face another problem. If different essences need features to distinguish them, and those features are all alike in being features, then the features themselves need a third kind of feature to distinguish them. The same question repeats without end. They are also forced to admit that a feature can itself be the subject of a statement, just as an essence can.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00324

Some people even avoid calling God “existent” or “nonexistent,” because “existent” is grammatically a passive form and they think God is too exalted for it. But wording is easy to handle when we are discussing knowledge and truth. Nearly all the words we apply to God—perhaps every one of them—carry a higher and nobler meaning when applied to Him than the ordinary meanings for which those words were first used. The authorized words “hearing” and “seeing,” for example, cannot mean bodily hearing and sight in God's case. The same is true of knowledge, power, existence, and will: their meaning for Him is higher and more perfect than what most people understand by those words. Still, we have to describe Him using familiar words that can carry more than one meaning, while making clear that His attributes are His very reality and are far beyond what we picture when we hear those words. This applies to His real attributes. For negative descriptions and relations, it is reasonable to use the ordinary meaning of the words.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00325

Anyone who argues that we should not call God “existent” because that would make Him share existence with created things has embraced pure negation. The same reasoning would prevent us from calling Him real, a being, or a thing, because these ideas also apply to other things. If He were not a thing, He would be nothing, since there is no third option between affirmation and denial. The same would follow for His reality, His identity, and His being established. This would close off every way of knowing Him or describing His beauty and perfection.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00326

It is astonishing that people who say such things are counted among serious scholars. I have included some of their confused arguments here for that very reason. Otherwise, no sensible person would spend time stating and answering them. In The Book of Discussions, Suhrawardi recounts their claims about nonexistent things being things and about a middle state. Their view leads to an even stranger result: they say the maker gives existence, yet existence itself is neither existent nor nonexistent. So the maker cannot give existence to existence, since that would bring the same problem back again. Nor can the maker establish existence, since, on their account, the thing was already established in itself through its possibility. What, then, did the maker give to essences? They have left the world without a creator.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00327

He says that such people appeared within the Muslim community. They were drawn to rational questions, but had neither sound judgment nor the kind of direct insight the mystics had. They came across books brought by a group during the Umayyad period, whose authors had names that sounded Greek. They assumed that anyone with a Greek name must be a philosopher. They found sayings in these books that appealed to them, developed them in the name of philosophy, and spread them widely, pleased with what they had found. Later thinkers followed them, even when they disagreed with some details. All of them were misled by the Greek names attached to works that seemed philosophical but contained no true philosophy. Their predecessors accepted these writings, and later generations followed them. Philosophy, he says, emerged only after the sayings of ordinary Greeks and their public speakers had spread and been accepted.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00328
Chapter — Relational existence
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00329

The term “relational existence” in philosophical discussions is used in two senses. One is the opposite of existence as a predicate: the way one thing exists in relation to another, as discussed when considering necessity, possibility, and impossibility. This is the link in affirmative statements, in addition to the judgment that joins subject and predicate—a judgment found in every kind of statement. Philosophers disagree about whether this linking existence differs in kind from existence as a predicate, and whether it occurs in simple statements such as “X exists.” The correct answers are yes to the first question and no to the second. In our view, existence has one nature throughout, but the meanings and abstract ideas drawn from it can differ in kind. As I will explain more fully, the truth is that the two agree only in the word “existence.”
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00330

The second sense is one way of considering a thing's existence as a feature of something else. It means that a thing is real in itself, but exists in something else, for something else, or in the presence of something else—not simply through itself. In our philosophy, only the Necessary Being, who exists through Himself, exists in this way for Himself. In the standard philosophical view, the immaterial beings that proceed through creation also do.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00331

For both views, the existence of an effect, considered as an effect, is the very existence it has through its complete efficient cause. But we say there is no aspect of the effect apart from its connection to its complete maker. This relation is the effect's existence; there is no separate existence on its side alongside the existence it has through its maker. In our view, effects are modes of existence brought about by direct creation. In the other view, an effect is either the essence itself, as the Stoics hold, or an essence described as existing, as the philosophers in Aristotle’s school hold. This dependent existence is not naturally different from a thing's existence in itself; it is simply one way of considering that existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00332

Now consider a different kind of link: the one between the subject and what we say about it in a statement. This does not mean the same thing as existence in itself. Take the sentence “whiteness exists in the body.” We can understand it in two ways. First, we can consider whiteness as existing in itself, even though it exists in a body. In that respect, we can say “Whiteness exists,” a simple statement about its existence. Second, we can consider whiteness as being present in the body. This is a different meaning from simply saying that whiteness exists, even though in reality it is the same whiteness considered under this relation. Only in the second sense can whiteness be the predicate of a compound statement such as “Whiteness exists in the body.” It means that whiteness is a feature of the body, existing for the body rather than for itself.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00333

Once we consider a feature as belonging to a subject in this way, we can relate it to either of two things. We may relate it to the feature itself and treat the connection as one of its states; or we may relate it to the thing that bears the feature and say, “The body has whiteness.” In that respect, the connection is one of the body's states.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00334

We also use “existence in itself” in two senses. In the first, it includes both what exists for itself and what exists in another, such as accidents and forms. This corresponds to the first sense of dependent existence. The second sense applies only to the existence a thing has in itself, not to features or attributes.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00335

In short, dependent existence in the first sense is a purely relational idea that cannot be understood on its own. It is like a grammatical link. We cannot strip away its linking role and turn it into an independent noun simply by directing our attention to it, as though it had become existence stated as a predicate. It may, however, be considered as a relation without being a linking expression. The second sense, by contrast, is an idea we can understand on its own: a thing's existence in itself. Its relation to something else is not part of the essence of the thing it belongs to, so we can consider it by itself and name it as an independent idea, unlike a pure relation.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00336

These distinctions also apply to nonexistence, as people have explained in the same way. Confusion often arises because the same word is used in different senses. If we agreed to call the first linking relation “linking existence” and the second “dependent existence,” and used “predicative existence” for the first independent sense and “existence in itself” for the second, we could avoid confusion. The same terminology could be used for nonexistence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00337
Method Two — The roots of necessity and possibility, and the parts of a statement
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00338
Chapter — Defining necessity, possibility, impossibility, truth, and falsehood
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00339

The mind grasps among its first ideas the meaning of necessity and its opposite, the absence of necessity. Some thinkers tried to define them precisely, rather than merely explain them. But their definitions went in a circle: they called the impossible what is not possible, then called the possible what is not impossible.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00340

They also defined what is necessary as something whose absence would lead to an impossibility, and what is possible as something whose presence or absence would lead to no impossibility. There is a flaw here, but not the one some people have pointed out. In the first definition, “possible” has the broad meaning; in the second, it has the narrow meaning. So those two definitions do not themselves form a circle. The problem lies elsewhere. To define the impossible as what must not exist is already to rely on the idea of what is necessary. The definitions therefore depend on each other.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00341

We should take these ideas from what is clear in itself. After the general ideas of existence and thinghood, the mind has no idea more basic than necessity and its absence. When necessity applies to existence, we call it necessity; when it applies to nonexistence, we call it impossibility. When necessity is absent from one side, we have possibility in the broad sense; when it is absent from both existence and nonexistence, we have possibility in the narrow sense.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00342

There is another flaw. A necessary thing is not one whose absence would cause some further impossibility. Its absence is itself impossible. No second impossibility is required. Sometimes none follows at all; sometimes what follows is no clearer than the impossibility of its absence. The same applies to what is impossible: the impossibility is the thing itself, not something that follows from supposing it to exist. Otherwise we would be defining a thing by the thing itself. Possibility is understood in the same way, as are all the broad ideas discussed in this field, as we have explained before.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00343

If you want to understand these three ideas, begin with necessity, which is clear in itself. Necessity is existence made firm, and existence is clearer than nonexistence: existence is known through itself, while nonexistence is known only in relation to existence. Then understand possibility as the absence of necessity on both sides, and impossibility as the necessity of nonexistence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00344

When philosophers first divided things into these three kinds, they considered how general essences relate, in thought, to existence and nonexistence. They had not yet considered the reality established by proof. They found that every general idea either calls for existence, calls for nonexistence, or calls for neither. This gave them three kinds: what is necessary in itself, what is possible in itself, and what is impossible in itself. The idea that something could call for both existence and nonexistence is ruled out as soon as we consider it. This is what they mean when they say the division into three is exhaustive by reason.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00345

But when they went on to examine things through proof, they found that it made no sense to suppose that an essence could require its own existence, even though that possibility had been included in their first conceptual division. So, at first, they defined what is necessary in this way.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00346

Once philosophers began explaining the features of what is necessary, another meaning of “necessary existence” became clear, as we will set out at the beginning of the next discussion. They sometimes use this teaching method for the sake of clarity. For example, they first establish the separate intellects, souls, and physical natures, and describe them as causes that bring about effects. They do so because they have already shown, in the proper place, that nothing truly acts in existence except the Necessary One. Any causal power or effect attributed to the other intellectual, spiritual, or natural principles is due to their role as conditions and preparations for the outpouring of the One, and to the many forms taken by His generosity and mercy.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00347

I follow the same method in many discussions. At first, and even in the middle of an argument, I take the philosophers' path. Only at the conclusion do I part ways with them. This gives readers a chance to become familiar with the argument before meeting ideas that might otherwise put them off. Just as the philosophers changed the meaning of “necessary” from what their initial definition led students to expect, we also change what people usually mean by “possible” in some cases outside the Necessary One, as you will see.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00348

Their books offer a more accurate division. Take anything that exists and consider it simply as existing, setting everything else aside. Can the mind call it “existent” on the basis of its own reality alone? Or must the mind also consider something else—a relation, something joined to it, or another feature?
